# Attained variable-shape extraction and permissible deformation conditions

This note proves attainment of the variable-shape extraction problem and
two concrete deformation statements. It does NOT prove that the optimal
retained mass reaches M/2^n. The competing integer centroid bases remain
separate feasible components; no derivative across those components is
assumed.

Let C be an ambient convex body in R^n x R^d, and put

    S=C intersect Lambda, Lambda=Z^n x R^d,
    q=dim_H(S)>0, mu=H_q|S, M=mu(S),
    P={z: H_q(C_z)>0}.

For a convex body D subset C with positive H_q mixed mass, write mu_D
for H_q restricted to D intersect Lambda, m_D=mu_D(S), and g_D for its
TRUE full ambient centroid. For a fixed beta, let F_beta consist of
such D for which g_D has integer base and

    mu_D(H)>=beta m_D

for every closed ambient halfspace containing g_D.

## 1. The maximum is attained by an actual ambient convex body

If F_beta is nonempty, then

    sup_(D in F_beta) m_D

is attained. In particular F_(gamma_d) is nonempty, and its maximum is
at least max_(z in P) H_q(C_z).

For the last assertion, retain one full positive fiber C_z by intersecting
C with a base box of radius less than 1/2 about z. This is an ambient
convex body: the open box contains a point of C, and int(C) approaches
every point of C. Its only integer fiber is C_z. Its true centroid has
integer base z and its local depth is at least gamma_q>=gamma_d by the
ordinary q-dimensional Grünbaum theorem. Restrictions of ambient
halfspaces to its q-affine span give exactly the required comparison.

Here is the attainment proof. Take a maximizing sequence D_l. The integer
base of each centroid lies in the finite integer projection of C, so pass
to a subsequence with a fixed centroid base j. For each z in the finite
set P, pass further to a fixed pattern in which the fiber (D_l)_z is
always empty or always nonempty. Every nonempty such fiber is a compact
convex subset of the FIXED q-dimensional affine space aff(C_z). Blaschke
selection in that space, followed by a finite diagonal subsequence,
gives compact convex Hausdorff limits L_z for all nonempty fibers.

Hausdorff convergence of compact convex sets inside a fixed bounded
q-affine space implies convergence of their indicators in L^1(H_q),
including when the limit has lower dimension. For a positive-volume
limit, indicators converge away from its null boundary; if the limit
is lower-dimensional, all approximants lie in shrinking neighborhoods
of a q-null compact set. Thus the mixed measures converge in TOTAL
VARIATION to

    mu_* = sum_z H_q restricted to ({z} times L_z),   (1)

where empty-pattern fibers contribute zero. Fibers of C outside P are
H_q-null and contribute nothing throughout. Mass and all first moments
converge. The limiting mass m_*>0 because the feasible sequence has a
positive feasible lower bound. Its centroid is g_*=(j,c_*).

The cap-depth condition survives without a boundary-null assumption.
For a closed halfspace H={a dot y>=b} containing g_*, use its outward
shift H_epsilon={a dot y>=b-epsilon}. It contains g_(D_l) for all large
l. Total-variation convergence gives mu_*(H_epsilon)>=beta m_*.
Let epsilon decrease to zero; continuity from above of a finite measure
gives mu_*(H)>=beta m_*.

It remains to realize (1) by an actual convex body; an ambient Hausdorff
limit alone would not suffice because new boundary integer fibers can
gain mass. Let D_0 be the convex hull of all lifted nonempty L_z.
For every z in P, its fiber equals L_z in the nonempty pattern and is
empty in the empty pattern. To prove this, express any point in a fiber
of the hull as a finite convex combination of limit fiber points and
approximate those points in the corresponding fibers of D_l, using the
SAME coefficients. The base remains exactly z. Convexity places the
approximants in (D_l)_z. An empty-pattern fiber is therefore impossible;
otherwise Hausdorff convergence places the limit in L_z. The reverse
inclusion is immediate from the hull construction.

Now discard zero-volume L_z as hull generators. The resulting compact
convex D_1 retains every positive L_z exactly and can only decrease
zero-volume fibers, so its mixed measure is still mu_*. Let P_* be its
positive-volume base set, and A=aff(P_*). The centroid base j is a
positive weighted average of all P_* and lies in ri(conv(P_*)).

If A=R^n, j lies in int(pi(C)). Every such integer base of an ambient
convex body has a full d-dimensional fiber, so q=d. A positive d-fiber
of D_1 together with n independent base directions forces D_1 to have
ambient dimension n+d. It is then the required actual convex body.

If A is proper, use the exact one-sided thickening lemma in
`candidate b90a2673d60a00b3`, Section 7;
its construction does not require symmetry once the proper base affine
span is given. Explicitly, choose a small interior ball B of C near a
point of D_1, strictly on one side of a base hyperplane containing A.
Choose its base distance to A smaller than the positive minimum distance
of all integer bases of C outside A. Then D=conv(D_1 union B) is an
ambient convex body, all of its integer bases lie in A, and its slices
over A equal D_1 exactly. Hence mu_D=mu_*. Its true centroid and every
cap mass are unchanged. This completes attainment.

## 2. Integer-centroid geometry and competing bases

For any positive feasible D, its centroid base j belongs to P. Indeed
write its centroid as the positive weighted average of its positive
fiber centroids. Convexity puts their weighted Minkowski average inside
D_j; it has dimension at least q. Since C_j has dimension at most q,
D_j has positive q-volume. This also forces all positive fibers of D
to have a common q-dimensional direction space: their weighted Minkowski
sum has direction equal to the sum of their direction spaces and still
has dimension at most q.

For each fixed j in P, the same compactification proves attainment of
the corresponding nonempty fixed-base problem. Thus the global optimum
is the maximum of finitely many attained fixed-base values. For
beta=gamma_d, every fixed-base problem is nonempty by the single-fiber
construction, and its value is at least H_q(C_j).

Every retained mass at fixed j is also bounded by the elementary
base-moment capacity

    T_j=max{sum_z t_z:0<=t_z<=H_q(C_z),
                         sum_z (z-j)t_z=0}.          (2)

The local-depth condition is an additional constraint; equality with
T_j is not claimed. None of these finite comparisons proves that some
feasible mass reaches M/2^n.

There is also an unconditional weaker retained-mass bound. The exact
parity correlation identity in
`candidate 93cf42ea22bcd767`
gives a reflection center retaining at least
`sum_r M_r^2/(2^q M)>=M/2^(n+q)`. Its symmetric intersection, with
exact ambient thickening if needed, is an actual extraction whose true
integer-base centroid has local half-depth. Therefore, since
gamma_d<=1/2,

    max_(D in F_(gamma_d)) m_D
       >=max{max_(z in P)H_q(C_z),
              sum_r M_r^2/(2^q M)}.

The extra factor 2^q in this proved bound is not removed here.

## 3. An exact depth-preserving family of permissible transformations

Let D be a maximizing body, with mass m and centroid g=(j,c). For s>0,
a real d-by-n matrix B, and b in R^d define

    T_(s,B,b)(z,x)=(z, b+B(z-j)+s(x-c)).               (3)

This is an affine bijection preserving Lambda. Each q-dimensional
integer fiber scales its measure by exactly s^q, independent of its
orientation. It suffices to impose only the positive INTEGER fiber fits

    b+B(z-j)+s(D_z-c) subset C_z,  z in P_D,          (4a)

where P_D is D's positive fiber set. Indeed P_D is lattice-convex by
Minkowski inclusion, so its convex hull has no additional integer bases.
The transformed positive-fiber hull is compatible and has exactly those
transformed fibers. It lies in C by (4a). If their base affine span is
full, the same integer-centroid argument as in Section 1 gives q=d and
an ambient body. Otherwise the exact one-sided thickening makes an
ambient body with unchanged integer traces. Thus there exists an actual
body D' subset C with precisely the transformed positive-fiber measure.
Its mass, true centroid and normalized depth are

    mass(D')=s^q m,
    true centroid(D')=(j,b),
    normalized depth_(D')((j,b))=depth_D((j,c)).       (4)

The last equality follows because the affine bijection maps all closed
ambient halfspaces bijectively; it is not a centroid inequality.
Consequently EVERY feasible transformation (3) at a maximizing D has

    s<=1.                                           (5)

This is a genuinely permissible deformation for arbitrary q>0. Its
source feasibility is explicit and is not presumed: (4a) is equivalent to

    u dot[b+B(z-j)+s(x-c)]<=h_(C_z)(u)               (6)

for all z in P_D, x in D_z and unit continuous normals u. No artificial
support contact at a noninteger base is used in these constraints.

## 4. Finite approximate contact stress without constraint qualification

Let m_0=dim aff(P_D). The saturation (5) implies the following rigorous
finite certificates. For every epsilon>0 there are at most

    d(m_0+1)+2

triples `((z_i,x_i),u_i,lambda_i)`, with z_i in P_D, x_i in D_(z_i),
unit continuous normals u_i, and lambda_i>=0, such that

    sum_i lambda_i u_i=0,
    sum_i lambda_i u_i(z_i-j)^T=0,
    sum_i lambda_i u_i dot(x_i-c)=1,                 (7)

and

    0<=sum_i lambda_i Delta_i<epsilon,
    Delta_i=h_(C_(z_i))(u_i)-u_i dot x_i>=0.          (8)

Proof: write delta_s=s-1 and delta_b=b-c. Constraint (6) becomes the
linear inequality

    delta_s u dot(x-c)+u dot B(z-j)+u dot delta_b
      <=Delta(u,z,x).                                (9)

Restrict B to the linear span of P_D-j, using any orthonormal coordinates
there; components outside it do not affect a source fiber. The effective
parameter dimension is p=1+d*m_0+d. The full intersection is feasible
at zero and has maximum delta_s equal to zero by (5).

A finite initial collection of valid inequalities makes the parameter
set bounded. Choose two distinct points in one positive fiber (possible
because q>0), and at least one point at each of m_0+1 affinely independent
bases from P_D. Constrain every continuous coordinate of their images
above and below by the corresponding support bounds of their C_z.
These are instances of (9) with normals +/-e_l. The evaluation map is
injective: subtracting the two equations in the one fiber forces
delta_s=0; the m_0+1 base equations then force B=0 and delta_b=0.
Bounded images therefore give bounded parameters.

Intersect this compact initial feasible set with delta_s>=epsilon.
The entire family (9) has empty intersection there. Compactness gives
a FINITE further subfamily already excluding it. The resulting finite
linear program is feasible and bounded, with optimal value in [0,epsilon).
Its standard finite LP dual gives nonnegative multipliers whose sum of
constraint gradients is the objective gradient and whose weighted slack
equals that optimal value. These are precisely (7)--(8). Conic
Caratheodory applied to the gradient-plus-slack vectors in R^(p+1)
reduces their number to at most p+1 while preserving every equation.

This argument does not assume differentiability, a Slater point, bounded
dual multipliers, or a closed limiting multiplier cone. In particular
the weights may diverge as epsilon decreases. No exact finite stress
supported solely on zero-slack contacts is inferred without an additional
constraint qualification. Equations (7)--(8) are the proved substitute.

## 5. A separate exact fiberwise Minkowski enlargement

Now assume q=d, and let P_D be the positive integer fiber set of D.
It is lattice-convex: every integer convex combination of its indices
supports a positive d-dimensional Minkowski combination of its fibers.
Thus `conv(P_D) intersect Z^n=P_D`.

For one common parameter 0<=t<=1 put

    E_z(t)=(1-t)D_z+t C_z,   z in P_D.               (10)

These fibers form a compatible family. Whenever w=sum lambda_z z is
integer, convexity of BOTH original bodies gives

    sum lambda_z E_z(t)
      subset (1-t)D_w+t C_w=E_w(t).

The convex hull of their lifts is contained in C and has exactly E_z(t)
at every integer base in P_D; its projection is conv(P_D), so there are
no other integer fibers. If its base hull has deficient rank, the same
one-sided thickening makes an ambient body with exactly these traces.

Every fiber and the resulting mixed measure increase with t, since
D_z subset C_z. The base centroid generally DRIFTS. Writing w_z(t) for
its volumes and m(t)=sum w_z(t), its base centroid is exactly

    j(t)=sum_z z w_z(t)/m(t).                        (11)

When derivatives exist, in particular for polytopes by the volume
polynomial for Minkowski combinations,

    j'(0)=m(0)^(-1) sum_z (z-j(0))w_z'(0).           (12)

For full-dimensional convex fibers the usual first mixed-volume formula
gives

    w_z'(0)=d[V(D_z[d-1],C_z)-|D_z|]>=0.             (13)

Equations (11)--(13) explicitly retain the base-moment obstruction. Even
equal base centroids at t=0 and t=1 do not justify deleting the intermediate
moment conditions. This flow is different from the ambient Minkowski sum,
which mixes real and integer bases in its fibers.

Here is an exact example of that drift, with n=1,d=2 and bases -1,0,1.
Let both endpoint fibers of D be the unit square, and let
`D_0=C_0=[0,3] times [0,3/2]`. Set
`C_-1=[0,4] times [0,1]` and `C_1=[0,2] times [0,2]`.
The endpoint Minkowski midpoint for C is exactly C_0; the smaller
endpoint midpoint for D lies in D_0. Their lifted hulls are therefore
actual convex bodies with precisely the displayed fibers, and D subset C.
Both original base centroids are zero because their endpoint areas agree.
Along (10), however,

    w_-1(t)=1+3t, w_0(t)=9/2, w_1(t)=(1+t)^2,
    j(t)=(t^2-t)/(13/2+5t+t^2)<0 for 0<t<1.

This is a base-moment counterexample only; no local-depth claim about
these particular D and C is needed.

## 6. Exact slack cost for an integer-balanced enlarging path

Still assume q=d. Suppose a path of actual subbodies D' subset C
enlarges all positive fibers of D and has the SAME integer centroid
base j; let its added mass be delta>=0 and its centroid be (j,c').
The exact moment relation is

    c'-c=(integral_(D'\D) (x-c)dmu)/(m+delta).        (14)

Let R_0 bound |x-c| on the added source, and let L_0 be a finite upper
bound on the sum, over original positive fibers, of all their
(d-1)-dimensional hyperplane section volumes. Such a bound is finite
by enclosing the finitely many fibers in fixed Euclidean balls; for
d=1 one may take their number. Then

    |c'-c|<=R_0 delta/(m+delta).                     (15)

For any nonvertical cap, changing its continuous center from c to c'
moves its unit-continuous-normal threshold by at most |c'-c|. Coarea
bounds its LOST original mass by L_0|c'-c|. This bound is uniform in
the integer tilt. Vertical caps do not change because the base j is
fixed. Added mass is nonnegative for every cap.

If the original depth constraint has uniform absolute slack

    sigma=inf_(H contains (j,c)) [mu_D(H)-beta m]>=0,

then D' remains feasible whenever

    beta delta+L_0 R_0 delta/(m+delta)<=sigma.        (16)

This gives an explicit mass-versus-centroid-motion budget for any
ACTUALLY integer-balanced enlargement, including (10) when its exact
moments (11) stay at j. It does not assert the existence of such a
balanced path. In particular a maximizing extracted body admitting
a nontrivial arbitrarily small balanced enlargement cannot have
positive uniform slack sigma. No unproved mixed centroid theorem or
cap/section law comparison is used in this conclusion.

The attainment, exact affine invariance, finite approximate contacts,
and slack cost are necessary structure for an extremal extraction.
They do not establish the sought retained fraction or resolve OC.
